claim: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses HIV viral load and restores lymphocyte responses to pathogen-derived antigens.
source: The efficacy with which antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses HIV viral load and restores lymphocyte responses to pathogen-derived antigens, normally lost due to viral replication, is well established (Cooney, 2002; Autran et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Cooney, 2002; Autran et al., 1997)

claim: Following ART initiation, CD4+ T-cell counts rapidly increase for approximately 4–6 months.
source: Following ART initiation, for the majority of HIV-infected individuals, the CD4+ T-cell counts rapidly increase for approximately 4–6 months (Lawn et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lawn et al., 2006

claim: After the initial rapid increase, CD4+ T-cell counts show a slower increase in the next 2–4 years.
source: Following ART initiation, for the majority of HIV-infected individuals, the CD4+ T-cell counts rapidly increase for approximately 4–6 months (Lawn et al., 2006), followed by a slower increase in the next 2–4 years
evidence: Supported by citation to Lawn et al., 2006

claim: CD4+ T-cell counts plateau after 2-4 years following ART initiation.
source: followed by a slower increase in the next 2–4 years, after which cell numbers plateau (Pinzone et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pinzone et al., 2012

claim: Approximately 10–16% of children on ART in Sub-Saharan Africa fail to suppress viral load within 12 months of ART initiation.
source: In Sub-Saharan Africa, approximately 10–16% of children on ART (Mutwa et al., 2014) and variable proportions of adults (Barth et al., 2011; Fatti et al., 2014; Mee et al., 2008) fail to suppress viral load within 12 months of ART initiation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mutwa et al., 2014

claim: Variable proportions of adults in Sub-Saharan Africa fail to suppress viral load within 12 months of ART initiation.
source: In Sub-Saharan Africa, approximately 10–16% of children on ART (Mutwa et al., 2014) and variable proportions of adults (Barth et al., 2011; Fatti et al., 2014; Mee et al., 2008) fail to suppress viral load within 12 months of ART initiation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barth et al., 2011; Fatti et al., 2014; Mee et al., 2008

claim: Among patients who suppress viral load, 35–40% are suboptimal immunological responders who do not reach a CD4+ T-cell count greater than 500 cells/µL within 5 years.
source: Further, among those that do suppress viral load, many are suboptimal immunological responders (35–40%), that is, they do not reach a CD4+ T-cell count greater than 500 cells/µL within 5 years (Nakanjako, 2016; Swiss HIV Cohort Study et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakanjako, 2016; Swiss HIV Cohort Study et al., 2005

claim: Some patients demonstrate no improvement in CD4+ T-cell counts at all following ART initiation.
source: Some patients demonstrate no improvement at all (Lawn et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lawn et al., 2006

claim: Generalized linear mixed models and generalized estimating equations are the most commonly used statistical methods in sub-Saharan African studies of CD4+ T-cell recovery.
source: A prior review of sub-Saharan African studies of this type established that generalized linear mixed models and generalized estimating equations were most commonly used (Sempa et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sempa et al., 2017

claim: Generalized linear mixed models and generalized estimating equations are not mechanistic models.
source: However, such models are not 'mechanistic', in the sense that they make no assumptions regarding the underlying biological processes involved in CD4+ T-cell reconstitution.
evidence: Based on the definition and characteristics of these statistical methods

claim: Non-mechanistic models do not allow inferences regarding the dynamics of CD4+ recovery.
source: For this reason, these methods do not allow inferences regarding the dynamics of CD4+ recovery.
evidence: Logical inference from the limitation of non-mechanistic models

claim: Recent studies have employed an asymptotic semi-mechanistic mixed model to describe CD4+ count recovery in children.
source: Recent studies have employed an asymptotic 'semi-mechanistic' mixed model to describe CD4+ count recovery in children (Lewis et al., 2012; ARROW Trial Team et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2017; De Beaudrap et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2012; ARROW Trial Team et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2017; De Beaudrap et al., 2008

claim: Recent studies have employed an asymptotic semi-mechanistic mixed model to describe CD4+ count recovery in adults.
source: Recent studies have employed an asymptotic 'semi-mechanistic' mixed model to describe CD4+ count recovery in children (Lewis et al., 2012; ARROW Trial Team et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2017; De Beaudrap et al., 2008) and adults (ANRS 1215/90 Study Group et al., 2009; Means et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to ANRS 1215/90 Study Group et al., 2009; Means et al., 2016

claim: In patients with suboptimal or no immune recovery, response trajectories do not follow an asymptotic recovery profile.
source: However, it has been demonstrated that in patients with suboptimal or no immune recovery, response trajectories do not follow this profile (ARROW Trial Team et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to ARROW Trial Team et al., 2013

claim: There is large natural variability of CD4+ T-cell counts across different population groups.
source: Complicating this picture, diverse CD4+ T-cell count variable transformations were applied, different demographic groups were studied and there is large natural variability of such cell counts across different population groups (Schaberg et al., 1997; Abuye et al., 2005; Maini et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schaberg et al., 1997; Abuye et al., 2005; Maini et al., 1996

claim: The study analyzed data from 1616 children with a median age of 4.3 years at ART initiation.
source: We use mixed-effects regression to fit the model to data from 1616 children (median age 4.3 years at ART initiation)
evidence: Data from the study cohort

claim: The study analyzed data from 14,542 adults with a median age of 36 years at ART initiation.
source: We use mixed-effects regression to fit the model to data from 1616 children (median age 4.3 years at ART initiation) and 14,542 adults (median age 36 years at ART initiation).
evidence: Data from the study cohort

claim: The scaled carrying capacity was closer to healthy values in children than in adults.
source: We found that the scaled carrying capacity, maximum CD4+ count relative to an HIV-negative individual of similar age, and baseline scaled CD4+ counts were closer to healthy values in children than in adults.
evidence: Results from the model fitting to study data

claim: Baseline scaled CD4+ counts were closer to healthy values in children than in adults.
source: We found that the scaled carrying capacity, maximum CD4+ count relative to an HIV-negative individual of similar age, and baseline scaled CD4+ counts were closer to healthy values in children than in adults.
evidence: Results from the model fitting to study data

claim: Post-ART initiation, CD4+ growth rate was inversely correlated with baseline CD4+ T-cell counts.
source: Post-ART initiation, CD4+ growth rate was inversely correlated with baseline CD4+ T-cell counts
evidence: Results from the model fitting to study data

claim: CD4+ growth rate post-ART was higher in adults than children.
source: Post-ART initiation, CD4+ growth rate was inversely correlated with baseline CD4+ T-cell counts, and consequently higher in adults than children.
evidence: Results from the model fitting to study data, inferred from inverse correlation with baseline counts

claim: De-identified longitudinal data from HIV-infected patients receiving ART in 13 South African cohorts was provided by IeDEA-SA.
source: De-identified longitudinal data from HIV-infected patients receiving ART in 13 South African cohorts was provided by the International Epidemiologic Databases to Evaluate AIDS in Southern Africa (IeDEA-SA) (https://www.iedea-sa.org/) (ART-LINC Collaboration of IeDEA et al., 2008; IeDEA and COHERE Cohort Collaborations and Anderegg, 2018).
evidence: Description of data source with citations

claim: The initial data set was composed of 2,858,743 CD4+ count observations for 223,688 patients.
source: The initial data set was composed of 2,858,743 CD4+ count observations for 223,688 patients of whom 202,108 were adults, 21,267 were children and 313 had no recorded date of birth or date of ART initiation.
evidence: Description of the study dataset

claim: After removing observations that were unrealistic or missing date of measurement, 189,647 adults and 19,060 children remained.
source: After removing observations that were unrealistic (outside plausible biological ranges) or missing date of measurement, 189,647 adults and 19,060 children remained (Figure 1).
evidence: Description of data cleaning process shown in Figure 1

claim: The logistic growth model assumes that a given quantity grows exponentially until it approaches a constant carrying capacity k.
source: This model assumes that a given quantity grows exponentially until it approaches a constant carrying capacity k (Figure 2), or limit, to represent the dynamics of the immune system.
evidence: Definition of the logistic growth model with reference to Figure 2

claim: The logistic growth model concept has been used in prior studies to describe the proliferation rate of CD4+ T-cells for individuals on therapy.
source: This concept has been used in prior studies to describe the proliferation rate of CD4+ T-cells for individuals on therapy (Kaufmann et al., 2001; Di Mascio et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaufmann et al., 2001; Di Mascio et al., 2006

claim: A study on healthy South African population showed that their CD4+ counts increased from young adulthood until about 70 years of age.
source: A study on healthy South African population showed that their CD4+ counts increased from young adulthood until about 70 years of age (Malaza et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Malaza et al., 2013

claim: When the value of K is close to unity, the patient's long-term carrying capacity is approaching the patient's homeostatic optimum for CD4+ T-cell counts.
source: An implication of this model is that when the value of K is close to unity, the patient's long-term carrying capacity is approaching the particular patient's 'homeostatic optimum' for CD4+ T-cell counts, that is, the amount of CD4 cells that can be sustained by the available biological resources.
evidence: Interpretation of the model parameter K based on the model structure

claim: When K is close to unity, a subsequent increase in CD4+ T-cell counts would be unlikely.
source: In this case a subsequent increase in CD4+ T-cell counts would be unlikely.
evidence: Logical inference from the model when K approaches unity

claim: In healthy adults, the value of Q would tend to unity due to an immune set-point.
source: Further, associated with an 'immune set-point' achieved in healthy adults their value of Q would tend to unity.
evidence: Inference based on biological understanding of healthy adult immune systems

claim: In healthy children, Q is expected to be less than one due to growth and changes in total blood volume.
source: In healthy children, this is not so owing to growth, that is, their CD4+ T-cell count changes with the increase of their total blood volume (Bains et al., 2009). Thus, their value of Q is expected to be less than one.
evidence: Inference based on biological understanding of child development, supported by citation to Bains et al., 2009

claim: A baseline scaled CD4+ T-cell count of 1 means that the individual started therapy with a normal CD4+ T-cell count for their age.

claim: The ratio model is likely to be better in accurately predicting the long-term behaviour of CD4+ T-cell counts trajectory.
source: Thus, it is likely to be better in accurately predicting the long-term behaviour of CD4+ T-cell counts trajectory.
evidence: Inference based on model's ability to reproduce known biological phases

claim: The ratio model is derived directly from the logistic growth model which describes a known biological process.
source: Furthermore, the ratio model is derived directly from the logistic growth model which describes a known biological process
evidence: Description of model derivation

claim: Larger values of baseline scaled CD4+ T-cell counts are associated with larger values of scaled CD4+ T-cell counts at any subsequent time.

evidence: Result from model fitting to data

claim: Higher baseline CD4+ T-cell counts are associated with a higher final or plateauing value for CD4+ T-cell counts.

evidence: Supported by citation to Moore and Keruly, 2007

claim: Patients with very low baseline CD4+ T-cell counts (<350 cells/µL) often fail to reach normal values even after long durations of therapy.

evidence: Supported by citations to Nakanjako, 2016; Swiss HIV Cohort Study et al., 2005; Moore and Keruly, 2007; Kelley et al., 2009

claim: The scaled carrying capacity of CD4+ T-cells in HIV-infected individuals was negatively correlated with the baseline scaled CD4+ T-cell counts in adults (−0.64) and children (−0.81).

evidence: Correlation analysis from model results

claim: The closer an individual is to their normal or optimal CD4+ T-cell value at ART initiation, the less cell population expansion is required to reach normal levels.
source: This seems reasonable in that the closer an individual is to their normal or optimal CD4+ T-cell value at ART initiation, the less cell population expansion is required to reach normal levels.
evidence: Logical inference from the negative correlation between carrying capacity and baseline counts

claim: The scaled cellular carrying capacity was higher in individuals on ART than in those who were healthy.

evidence: Comparison of model parameter estimates

claim: In both HIV-infected adults and children the scaled carrying capacity post-ART was greater than 1.
source: In both HIV-infected adults and children the scaled carrying capacity post-ART was greater than 1

claim: Baseline CD4+ T-cell counts were lower than their corresponding long-term homeostatic optimum in HIV-infected individuals.

evidence: Interpretation of scaled carrying capacity > 1

claim: Individual CD4+ T-cell counts had to grow to reach normal levels in HIV-infected individuals on ART.
source: That is, individual CD4+ T-cell counts had to grow to reach normal levels.
evidence: Interpretation of scaled carrying capacity > 1

claim: An impaired immune system usually experiences repair following treatment initiation.
source: This is consistent with the notion that an impaired immune system usually experiences repair following treatment initiation.
evidence: Established biological understanding of ART effects

claim: In healthy children, CD4+ T-cell counts increase until the age of approximately 1 year and then decrease thereafter.

claim: Total blood and body volume increase throughout childhood.
source: Total blood and body volume increase throughout childhood
evidence: Established biological knowledge of child development

claim: The combination of increasing blood volume and thymic shrinkage results in decreasing CD4+ T-cell counts per volume with age in children.

evidence: Inference from the combined effects of blood volume increase and thymic shrinkage

claim: A scaled carrying capacity of 0.49 in healthy adults suggests a decreasing CD4+ T-cell trend with age.

evidence: Interpretation of model parameter estimate

claim: CD4+ T-cell counts decreased from young adulthood to middle age in studies from elsewhere.

evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Table 4

claim: The higher the scaled CD4+ T-cell counts of an individual at ART initiation, the lower the rate of recovery will be.
source: This implies that the higher the scaled CD4+ T-cell counts of an individual at ART initiation, that is, the closer it is to its healthy/normal true value, the lower the rate of recovery will be.
evidence: Interpretation of the inverse correlation between baseline counts and growth rate

claim: The inverse relationship between baseline CD4+ counts and recovery rate is in agreement with the findings of prior studies.
source: This is reasonable given a decrease in the need to achieve normal levels and is in agreement with the findings of prior studies (Lawn et al., 2006; Sachsenberg et al., 1998).

claim: CD4+ T-cell growth rates were higher in individuals on ART than in healthy individuals.
source: We found that CD4+ T-cell growth rates were higher in individuals on ART than in healthy individuals.
evidence: Comparison of model parameter estimates

claim: Prior studies found that cell growth rates in adults on ART were sixfold to tenfold greater than in healthy adults.

evidence: Supported by citations to Sachsenberg et al., 1998; Hazenberg et al., 2000

claim: After treatment initiation, there is an initial redistribution of memory T-cells from the lymph nodes into the blood stream.

evidence: Supported by citation to Tsukamoto et al., 2009; Autran, 1999

claim: After treatment initiation, redistribution of memory T-cells is followed by homeostatic proliferation and production of naïve cells by the thymus.

source: Thus, post-ART CD4+ T-cell growth rate in HIV-infected individual might be smaller now than it may have been on average in the past, as CD4+ T-cell counts at ART initiation are now higher.
evidence: Speculation based on changes in treatment guidelines and the inverse relationship between baseline counts and growth rate

claim: Baseline scaled CD4+ T-cell count was lower in adults compared to children (0.2 vs 0.8).
source: Baseline scaled CD4+ T-cell count was lower in adults compared to children (0.2 vs 0.8)
evidence: Comparison of model parameter estimates

evidence: Inference based on knowledge of transmission routes and PMTCT programs

claim: Adults might be infected for an extended period and are consequently more likely to be more highly immune-compromised prior to diagnosis, compared to children.

evidence: Acknowledgment of potential limitation

claim: The subset used was representative of the full data set.
source: However, with the exception of the percentage of people that suppressed viral load within 12 months of starting ART (Table 1), comparison of the summary statistics of the subset versus the full data set demonstrated that they were similar. Further, the results obtained from adjusting and not adjusting the model parameters with the variable, viral load suppression within 12 months, were also in agreement (see Supplementary file 4). We consequently believe that the subset used was representative of the full data set.
evidence: Comparison of summary statistics and model results between subset and full dataset
